measured.lens: Blind photogrammetric measurement of a disassembled sheet-metal gripper jaw from 6 ruler-referenced photos. Scale established per photo by fitting a projective (Möbius) model x_px = (a·s+b)/(1+c·s) to the widest run of machine-detected 10 mm ruler ticks (residuals ≤0.5 px), then measuring the part by threshold segmentation + convex-hull diameter, row/column scans, and hand-verified zoom crops. No repo file was consulted for expected values.
findings: Photo inventory and overview: all six files are 4000x3000. Downscaled overviews written to the scratchpad show three distinct rest poses: part lying flat beside a VERTICAL ruler (KakaoTalk_...194.jpg = 'p00', and ..._02.jpg = 'p02'); part standing ON a HORIZONTAL ruler (..._04.jpg, ..._05.jpg); and two oblique 3/4 views (..._01.jpg, ..._03.jpg).

Ruler scale, p04 (horizontal ruler): the deepest tick tips were found by column-wise max-depth scan. Ten 10 mm marks located at x = 920.0, 1102.5, 1281.5, 1459.5, 1635.0, 1808.0, 1979.5, 2149.5, 2318.0, 2484.5 px. Widest labelled pair used = 10 mm to 100 mm (1564.5 px / 90 mm). Projective fit residual max 0.51 px. Local scale falls 18.26 -> 16.53 px/mm across the ruler (9% perspective gradient).

Ruler scale, p00 (vertical ruler): 10 mm marks at y = 1319.9(70), 1514.4(60), 1710.0(50), 1907.7(40), 2107.3(30), 2308.4(20). Widest pair = 20 to 70 mm (988.5 px / 50 mm). Fit residual max 0.21 px. Local scale 19.34 -> 20.21 px/mm (3.4% gradient), i.e. nearly orthographic.

Ruler scale, p02 (vertical ruler): 5 mm marks at y = 822.2(50) ... 1728.7(5). Widest pair = 5 to 50 mm (906.5 px / 45 mm). Fit residual max 0.39 px. Local scale 20.06 -> 20.25 px/mm, only 1% gradient over the whole ruler — p02 is the closest to orthographic of all six photos and is my primary measurement view.
Ruler scale, p05 (horizontal ruler): 5 mm marks at x = 1281.1(5) ... 1893.3(40). Widest pair = 5 to 40 mm (612.2 px / 35 mm). Fit residual max 0.09 px. Local scale 17.80 -> 17.20 px/mm.

Part topology, as seen: a laser-cut plate carrying a servo-horn pattern (one ~10 mm central circle with lobed satellites, plus a 15.1 mm rectangular U-notch, two ~3.5-4 mm holes on 25.5 mm centres, two ~2 mm holes, and a castellated/notched bottom edge), plus TWO long tapered blades. Each blade has an elongated through-slot and a rounded tip with a small opening.

UNRESOLVED 3D detail (affects item f): in every view where the plate is face-on (p00, p02, p05) exactly ONE blade shows its full flat face — the through-slot lets background light through, proving we see through the sheet — while the OTHER blade shows only a ~1.5 mm dark edge. Both blades' long axes are parallel and equal length in those same views. Geometrically this means the two blades' planes are roughly 90 deg apart (one blade coplanar with the plate, one bent out of the plate plane), not the symmetric parallel-flange U-channel I first assumed. I could not rule out that the part is simply bent/damaged. I checked the alternative explanation (both blades perpendicular, apparent width caused by off-axis perspective): it fails quantitatively — an 800 px off-axis blade at the estimated 150-250 mm camera distance would project only ~30-40 px of depth, not the ~90-150 px face actually observed.

Plate is genuinely face-on in p00: the isolated mounting hole measures 62 px wide x 63 px tall (w/h = 1.0), and independently the plate's left/right edge midpoint (x = 1650) matches the two mounting holes' symmetry axis (x = 1652.6) to within 3 px. Both confirm no meaningful foreshortening of the plate in p00.

Overall extent, p00 (part flat, plate face-on, part and ruler in the same table plane): convex-hull diameter 1715 px between plate apex (1706,1169) and blade tip (1178,2801). Converting the y-component through the ruler model (77.84 mm -> -4.11 mm) gives 81.95 mm, plus 26.5 mm in x, => 86.1 mm corner-to-corner. Along the part's long axis alone: 82.2 mm.

Overall extent, p02 (near-orthographic): part bbox x 543 -> 2245 px = 1702 px at 20.25 px/mm = 84.0 mm along the long axis; convex-hull diameter 1787 px = 88.0 mm corner-to-corner. Threshold sensitivity at the blurred blade tip is +/-10 px (~0.5 mm); values at thresholds 70/80/90 spanned 87.2-88.5 mm.

Overall extent, p04 (part STANDING on the ruler): raw x-span 753 -> 2139 px reads 78.5 mm on the ruler-plane scale. This DISAGREES with p00/p02 by ~6 mm and is doubly biased — the blade sits ~40 mm above the ruler (nearer the camera, magnified) while the part is also rotated about its vertical axis (foreshortened). I therefore reject p04 as an absolute-length source and keep p00/p02.

Plate size: width (across the two arms) = 720 px between x 1290 and 2010 at y 1465 in p00 => 37.0 mm; independently 651 px at the ruler plane in p05 => 37.4 mm. Height (apex to lowest bottom tab) = y 1160 -> 2005 in p00 via the ruler model (78.30 -> 35.11 mm) => 43.2 mm; independently in p02, plate apex x 2245 to arm tips x ~1360 = 885 px => 43.8 mm.

Blade free length (from where it leaves the plate to its tip): p02 gives x 1360 (plate arm tip) -> 543 (blade tip) = 817 px = 40.3 mm for the lower blade, and 877 px = 43.3 mm if the arm tip is taken at x 1420 where the notch ends. p00 gives 852 px along the blade axis = 42.6 mm. Consistency check: plate height 43 + blade 41 = 84 mm, which matches the measured 84.0 mm overall long-axis extent.

Blade count = 2. Their separation is measured most safely in p05, where both blade bases sit ON the ruler surface (zero height bias): outer-face-to-outer-face span = 678 px at y 1740-1780 = 38.6 mm. Subtracting one sheet thickness per side gives an inner clear gap of ~35.5 mm. Note the same span reads 42-43 mm when measured 30 mm higher up — that inflation (+12% over 31 mm of height) is exactly the standing-part perspective error and is the reason I used the base measurement only.

Sheet thickness: minimum apparent width of a blade seen edge-on. p02 upper blade minimum 31 px at 20.2 px/mm = 1.54 mm (median along its length 47 px = 2.33 mm, inflated because the blade is not perfectly edge-on). p05 right blade minimum 28 px at 17.2 px/mm = 1.63 mm. Both are upper bounds since dark-edge blur widens the segment; nominal 1.5 mm stock is the most likely true value.

Perspective/height model, measured not assumed: in p05 the across-blade span grows 38.6 -> 43.3 mm over 31 mm of height above the ruler, i.e. ~0.4%/mm, implying a camera distance of roughly 150-260 mm. This is the magnitude of error that would corrupt any dimension read off the ruler for a feature standing above it, and is why all primary numbers come from the two flat-lying photos.

Depth perpendicular to the plate (item f) has NO direct measurement: none of the six photos shows the plate edge-on against the ruler. Indirect estimate only — modelling the p05 right blade's apparent 50 px band as w*cos(alpha) + t*sin(alpha) with t = 1.5 mm gives alpha ~ 77 deg, so a blade of face width 6.5 mm projects ~6.3 mm of out-of-plane depth. I report 6-8 mm at LOW confidence.

Scale sanity anchors (not used to derive anything, only to check plausibility): the two isolated plate holes measure 3.3 x 3.9 mm and 3.3 x 4.0 mm on 25.5 mm centres (consistent with M3/M4 clearance), the central servo circle is ~10.0 mm, and the U-notch is 15.1 mm wide. All land on sensible hardware values, which supports the px->mm calibration.

caveats: I could NOT fully resolve the part's 3D topology. In all three views where the mounting plate is face-on (p00, p02, p05), one blade shows its full flat face (the through-slot passes light) while the other shows only a ~1.5 mm edge, even though both blades' long axes are parallel and equal in length. That means the two blades' planes are ~90 deg apart, not parallel as a U-channel bracket would be. I tested and quantitatively rejected the perspective explanation. I cannot tell from photos alone whether this is the design or whether the part is bent/damaged. This is the single biggest open question and it is what makes item (f) an estimate rather than a measurement.

Item (f) — depth perpendicular to the plate — is NOT directly measured. No photo places the plate edge-on next to the ruler. The 6-8 mm figure is inferred from a tilt model of one blade and should be treated as UNKNOWN-with-an-estimate.

Photos _04 and _05 have the part STANDING ON the ruler. I measured the resulting bias empirically in _05: the across-blade span grows from 38.6 mm at the ruler surface to 43.3 mm about 31 mm higher, i.e. roughly +0.4% per mm of height (camera distance ~150-260 mm). Any dimension of an elevated feature read directly off that ruler is therefore inflated by up to ~12-15%. I used _05 only for the base-plane span, and I rejected _04's 78.5 mm length outright — it disagrees with the two flat-lying photos by ~6 mm because it is both elevation-magnified and rotation-foreshortened.

Photos p00 and p02 have vertical rulers but the part's long axis is measured partly across the ruler direction, so those numbers assume isotropic image scale. I bounded that assumption from the ruler's own perspective gradient: 0.6% across the whole ruler in p02 and 3.4% in p00. p02 is therefore the better source; p00 may carry up to ~2-3% systematic error on cross-ruler distances.
The plate's far edge touches or overlaps the ruler in the image in both p00 and p02, so its exact outer boundary is uncertain by roughly +/-10 px (~0.5 mm).

Blade tips are thin and motion/focus blurred. Varying the segmentation threshold (70/80/90) moved the overall extent by 1.3 mm in p02 and by up to 4 mm in p00 (at threshold 70 the p00 tip was cut off entirely). I report the mid-threshold values and the spread.

Every dimension is a projection of a 3D object onto one image plane. Where the two endpoints of a measurement are at different depths, the projected length underestimates the true 3D distance. This applies most to the corner-to-corner figure in (a').
The camera focal length / distance was never measured; the perspective estimates (150-260 mm) come from the ruler's own scale gradient and are rough.

I did not read any project file, CAD, URDF, USD, STL or prior measurement before producing these numbers, per the blind-measurement instruction. I have not compared them against any expected value. Nothing in the repository was created, modified or accessed; all crops were written under the session scratchpad.

measured.lens: Blind photogrammetric read of a single disassembled flat plate against a steel mm rule. Only photo `KakaoTalk_20260806_210148446.jpg` (call it P00) has the part lying directly ON the rule blade, so it is the sole scale-bearing view; the other three are used for shape/topology confirmation and one independent ratio cross-check. Headline finding: the photographed part is a ONE-PIECE FLAT PLATE (base flange + triangular yoke arm + pivot eye). It has no fork, no pair of blades, and no through-thickness slot — so the premise "number of blades / gap between them / interleaved beak" does not have a positive answer for this object.
findings: Scale established in P00 only. The part rests directly on the rule blade there; in the other three photos the part is held above the table or lies on a different plane from the rule, so their absolute scale is not trustworthy and I did not use it for mm values.

px->mm anchor: the long cm tick under the '10' label sits at x=770.4 px, the long cm tick under '130' at x=2938.6 px (both verified by overlaying the detected tick on an 8x crop and reading the printed label — /tmp/.../crops/p00_label10.png, p00_label130.png). That is the widest confidently-readable labelled pair: 120 mm over 2168.2 px.

Because of perspective the pitch is NOT constant: it runs 17.55 px/mm at the left of the rule to 18.55 px/mm at the right. I fit a 1-D projective model x=(A*u+B)/(C*u+1) to 16 cm/half-cm ticks (A=17.3668, B=595.438, C=-2.23762e-4); RMS residual 0.53 px = 0.03 mm. Local horizontal scale across the part is 18.02 -> 18.35 px/mm.

Vertical scale differs from horizontal (the plate is not perfectly fronto-parallel). I recovered it from the aspect ratio of four circular holes read on 8x grids: dia_y/dia_x = 1.058, 1.081, 1.108, 1.083 (mean 1.083, sd 0.021). So S_y = 1.083 * S_x ~= 19.5-19.9 px/mm. All 'across' dimensions use this.

Part topology confirmed across all four photos: ONE flat plate. Decisive evidence — in P00 the rule's printed graduations and the words 'AL', '80', '90', 'NGLE' are clearly visible THROUGH both the large rectangular window and the triangular window (/tmp/.../crops/p00_grid.png, z_tri.png). If a second, parallel plate existed behind, those windows would be blocked. Nothing is behind.

Shape, from the mounting end to the far end: (1) a parallel-sided base flange carrying a large rounded-corner rectangular window, four ~3 mm corner holes, and an obround (slotted) cut-out at the extreme mounting end; (2) a shoulder where both long edges turn inward at roughly 40 deg; (3) a triangular yoke — the arm is split by a triangular through-window into two COPLANAR legs; (4) the legs converge on a rounded lobe carrying a single ~2.9 mm through-bore (a pivot eye).
The four ~3 mm holes are not a square pattern: 19.75 mm along the part axis by 23.49 mm across it. Both pairs straddle the rectangular window, which sits between them.

The obround slot is only visible in photo _03 (in P00 it is hidden behind the loose bolt/bearing hardware). Scaled by the hole-diameter ratio it is roughly 15.5 x 5.3 mm, lying across the axis at the extreme mounting end.

Independent cross-check between two photos with independent scales: plate across-width divided by mounting-hole diameter = 550/57.0 = 9.65 in P00, and 461/48.1 = 9.58 in photo _03 (where the hole images as a 48.1 x 38.9 px ellipse, giving that photo its own foreshortening correction). Those agree to 0.7%, i.e. 28.1 mm vs 28.3 mm. This is the strongest confidence anchor in the whole read.

Tip profile: a smooth CONVEX rounded lobe, essentially a semicircular clevis eye. No chisel bevel, no hook, no notch, no serration, no flat gripping pad, no rubber/pad seat, no counterbore. The bore centre sits 3.65 mm back from the extreme tip. The whole surface is uniformly coarse and granular (cast/sintered or heavily bead-blasted), which would add friction but is a finish, not a gripping geometry.

Sheet thickness could not be measured properly. Nothing in these four photos shows the plate edge-on against a scale. My only handle is the apparent 'overhang' band along the tip and lower edges in P00 (6-8 px), which is the parallax of the raised top face over the rule beneath. Converting that needs the camera focal length, which I have to assume (~2850-3200 px for a 4000 px phone frame). That yields 2.2-3.0 mm. Photo _01 shows a bright band along a tilted edge that, if it is the side face, would imply ~1.3 mm — I could not confirm whether that band is the side face or a lit chamfer, so the two estimates disagree and I am reporting thickness as weakly constrained.

There is no interleaving capability visible. The two 'legs' of the yoke are cut from the same single sheet and lie in the same plane; the gap between them (the triangular window, 15.3 mm across x 9.65 mm deep) opens sideways within the plate, not through its thickness. A mating jaw blade could only enter that opening by travelling normal to the sheet, which is not the direction a jaw closes. So: no interleaved-beak geometry on this part.

Honest mismatch flag: this object does not read as a gripping jaw. Four M3-class holes on a 19.75 x 23.49 mm rectangle, a big rectangular clearance window, an obround slot, and a lightened yoke ending in a single 2.9 mm pivot eye is the signature of a mounting flange / linkage plate. I found no gripping face anywhere on it. Either the fixed jaw is a different piece, or 'fixed jaw' here means the rigid frame plate that the moving jaw pivots on (the tip bore would then be the hinge-pin seat).

The bolt/bearing hardware in the frame is a separate loose item, not attached to the plate in any of the four views (in P00 it lies flat on the rule beside the plate, its axis in the image plane while the plate face is toward the camera — geometrically impossible if it passed through the plate). It is a threaded shank of about 10 mm OD and about 17 mm thread length, a bright hex nut about 15 mm across flats, a stack of black rings, a white nylon-insert nut, and a chromed spherical/dome end. These figures are inflated by the cylinder standing proud of the rule and are low precision.

caveats: PREMISE MISMATCH — read this first. The task described 'the FIXED jaw ... blades ... gap between them ... interleaved beak'. The object in these four photographs has none of that. It is a single flat plate: a parallel-sided mounting flange (4x ~3 mm holes on a 19.75 x 23.49 mm rectangle, a ~12.5 x 21.2 mm rectangular window, a ~15.5 x 5.3 mm obround slot) that tapers at a shoulder into a triangular yoke ending in one rounded lobe with a single ~2.9 mm through-bore. There is no gripping face, no fork, no tine pair. Either this is not the jaw, or 'fixed jaw' is being used to mean the rigid frame plate that the moving jaw hinges on. I did not assume either — I measured what is in frame.

Answer to the interleaving question: NO, not as photographed. Interleaving requires two blades separated in the thickness direction with a slot between them. This is one sheet ~2-3 mm thick. Its only openings are through-holes in the plane of the sheet; a mating blade could enter them only by moving normal to the sheet, which is not a jaw-closing direction. If the real gripper does interleave, the mating geometry is on a part not shown here.

Only photo `KakaoTalk_20260806_210148446.jpg` carries a valid scale. In it the part lies flat on the rule blade. In _01 and _02 the part is held above the table, closer to the camera than the rule (measured rule pitch there is 12.5-13.5 px/mm while the part images at roughly 17 px/mm), so any mm value taken from those photos would be ~25% too small. In _03 the part and the rule are on the same table but the part is strongly tilted (a circular hole images as a 48.1 x 38.9 px ellipse) and the rule is far from it; I used _03 only for a scale-free ratio cross-check, never for an absolute number.

Systematic bias not corrected: the plate sits ON TOP of the rule, so its top face is one sheet-thickness (~2-3 mm) closer to the camera than the graduations. At a plausible 300-400 mm camera distance this inflates every in-plane dimension by roughly 0.6-1.0%, i.e. about +0.3 mm on the 39 mm length. All quoted values are therefore very slightly large.

The vertical (across-axis) scale rests on assuming the four mounting holes and the tip bore are truly circular. Four independent holes gave dia_y/dia_x = 1.058-1.108 (mean 1.083, sd 0.021), so I used S_y = 1.083*S_x. If any hole is actually slotted or the plate has out-of-plane curvature, every 'across' number (28.1 mm height, 23.5 mm hole pitch, 21.2 mm window, 15.3 mm yoke opening) shifts proportionally. That +/-2% is already folded into the quoted tolerances.

Thickness is the weakest number in this report and I would not build anything on it. There is no edge-on view against a scale in any of the four photos. The 2.2-3.0 mm figure comes from a parallax-overhang model that needs an assumed camera focal length (I used 2856-3200 px). A bright band along a tilted edge in photo _01 would imply ~1.3 mm instead, and I could not determine whether that band is the true side face or a lit chamfer. Two features could not be measured in the well-calibrated photo: the fourth (lower-right) mounting hole and the obround slot are both occluded — by the photographer's finger and by the loose bolt/bearing assembly respectively. The obround slot value comes from photo _03 via the ratio method and carries about +/-1.5 mm.

The exact along-axis extent of the 'base plate' depends on where you declare the shoulder. I placed it at x=2215 px, where both long edges begin turning inward, read to about +/-20 px (+/-1.1 mm). That uncertainty transfers directly and oppositely between the 25.5 mm base length and the 13.7 mm arm length; their sum, 39.3 mm, is the well-determined quantity.

Photo _03 disagrees with P00 on the hole pattern: _03's ratio method makes both pitches about equal (~22.2 x 22.4 mm) whereas P00 gives 19.75 x 23.49 mm. _03 is strongly tilted with likely oblique (sheared) foreshortening that my axis-aligned correction cannot model, so I weighted P00. measured.lens: METRIC-SEMANTICS audit of the sealed G0b T3R Gate-0 visual-mesh audit: what l_vis operationally is in the script, what the JSON fields do and do not measure, and whether the measured facts entail the "source contains no distal jaw finger" proposition asserted in the 31st session doc and D427. Read-only; no re-run, no asset parsing, no writes to the repo.
findings: Q1 — l_vis operational definition, from source only (sim_scripts/g0b_t3r_gate0_visual_mesh_distal_depth_readonly_audit.py). POINT SET: `sample_triangles()` (L232-250) returns the raw STL triangle SOUP vertices (`tris_m.reshape(-1,3)`) PLUS a uniform barycentric lattice per triangle with subdivision n = ceil(max_edge / 0.0005 m) — i.e. SURFACE samples at <=0.5 mm pitch. No hulling, no interior, no volume. Sources are exactly two hardcoded files in `VIS_PINS` (L122-125): gripper_link.stl, link5.stl. FRAME: `depth_r_mm()` (L253-259) operates on points expressed in the link5 URDF frame; for link5 the STL sits at identity (GV2 gates visual origin xyz=0/rpy=0/scale=0.001, L442-448), for gripper_link the points are pushed through `gripper_T_l5(joint,q5) = T0 @ Rz(q5) @ inv(T1)` (L347-350) from the frozen attempt3 USD joint. REFERENCE PLANE: the plane z = TCP_LOCAL[2] = 0.115428 m in the link5 frame (L144), i.e. a plane NORMAL TO THE LINK5 +Z AXIS through the URDF `link5_to_hand_tcp` origin — not a point, not a sphere. SIGN: `depth = (z - 0.115428)*1000`, so POSITIVE = further along link5 +z = 'below TCP toward the object'; material above the TCP returns negative depth. WINDOW: `l_vis_mm()` (L262-264) masks `r <= 30.0 mm` where `r = hypot(x,y)*1000` about the link5 z-axis through x=y=0. The window is an INFINITE cylinder: it is unbounded in depth in BOTH directions and has no azimuthal or axial restriction. MAXIMISATION: `depth[m].max()` — a single scalar = the depth of the single deepest sampled point inside that cylinder (ties resolved by numpy argmax first-index, which is exactly the near-axis tie-break degeneracy the 31st doc §3 note flags). For the fixed body it is evaluated once (pose-free, L505-506). For the moving body it is additionally maximised over q5: coarse grid `[88.3100] + arange(88.0, -0.001, -0.25)` (L522), then a refine grid `arange(argmax-1.0, argmax+1.0, 0.02)` (L531-533), and the REFINED argmax is what the gate consumes (L540). Verdict rule `tri_state()` (L322-327): PASS if l_vis > 6.0, FAIL if l_vis < 5.0, else INDETERMINATE; any FAIL -> GATE0_SOURCE_ABSENT (L609-614). So l_vis is, in one sentence: the maximum signed protrusion of surface samples past one authored plane, inside one radial cylinder, maximised over one joint angle.

Q2 — `moving_gripper_link.peak_point.body_frame_m` = [0.06708260, -0.00598342, -0.01893356] m. MEANING: `peak_point(d_pk, r_pk, pts_pk, grip_pts_g)` (L547) passes `grip_pts_g` as the fourth argument, and `grip_pts_g` is the UNTRANSFORMED sampled mesh (L521: `meshes['gripper_link']['pts']` = binary STL coords x 0.001). So body_frame_m is the same physical point expressed in gripper_link's OWN mesh/link frame (identical to the URDF link frame because GV2 gated the visual origin to identity). It is NOT a tool-frame coordinate and NOT comparable to the depth/r numbers. The companion `tool_frame_m` = [3.215e-06, -1.1257e-04, 0.11938392] m reproduces depth = (0.11938392-0.115428)*1000 = 3.9559 mm and r = 0.1126 mm exactly. DISTANCE FROM BODY ORIGIN: |(67.083, -5.983, -18.934) mm| = 69.96 mm. COMPARISON TO mesh_stats.gripper_link.bbox_mm = [77.850, 25.240, 39.368]: the bbox DIAGONAL is 90.816 mm (the same 90.8 mm the script itself quotes in `depth_error_bound_derivation`), so the peak point sits at 77.0% of the body's full diagonal extent from its own origin, and its x-coordinate alone is 86.2% of the body's longest extent (77.850 mm). CONSEQUENCE: the point that produced the verdict-driving peak depth is a far-field, distal-end feature of the moving jaw mesh — NOT a near-origin artefact. The metric did in fact latch onto the tip of the jaw lever. What it reports is that this tip, at its best sweep pose (q5=5.10 deg, near-closed), lands 0.113 mm from the tool axis and only 3.956 mm past the TCP plane. Caveat: mesh_stats records EXTENTS only, not min/max coordinates, so the point cannot be pinned to a specific bbox face from the JSON alone.

Q3 — Shape/extent fields in the JSON: essentially none that bear on the verdict. Exhaustive sweep of the JSON: (a) `mesh_stats.<body>.bbox_mm` is the ONLY true extent measurement — an axis-aligned whole-body bbox in the body's own frame. It is computed inside the GV3 units-sanity gate (script L467-468: `ok = all(bbox > 0.005) and all(bbox < 0.4)`) and reused only for the angular error bound; it never enters `tri_state`, it is whole-body (cannot isolate a finger), and it is not tool-frame. (b) `peak_point.{r_mm, azimuth_deg, tool_frame_m, body_frame_m}` and `r_at_l_vis_mm` localise ONE point — position, not extent or silhouette. (c) `max_depth_in_footprint_mm` (r<=14.5), `max_depth_in_wall_annulus_mm` (12.5<=r<=20) and `l_vis_mm` (r<=30) form a 3-band radial decomposition — the closest thing to shape in the JSON — but each band still reports a MAX DEPTH RELATIVE TO THE TCP PLANE. (d) `n_pts_in_rim_band` / `min_r_mm_in_rim_band`: note `rim = (depth>=5.0)&(depth<=15.0)` in `body_metrics()` (L271) has NO radius restriction, so `n_pts_in_rim_band=0` is an all-radii statement — but it is still a depth-band occupancy count, not an extent. VERDICT ON Q3: every field that can move the verdict is a max-depth-relative-to-the-TCP-plane statistic. No field measures span, silhouette, projected area, finger width, protrusion direction, or thickness. The sibling artifact `t3r_gate0_vismesh_bands.csv` (70 rows x 8 poses) does carry a partial radial PROFILE (per 0.5 mm depth band: n_pts, min_r, max_r inside r<=30), which is the nearest thing to a silhouette anywhere in the run — but it too is indexed by depth relative to the TCP plane, and it is clipped to depth in [-5, +30] mm and r <= 30 mm, so it cannot see the body above -5 mm depth either.

Q4 — STRICT LOGIC: the measured facts entail P2, not P1. P2 as actually established: 'Among <=0.5 mm-pitch surface samples of the two URDF-pinned visual STLs, expressed in the link5 frame, no sample lies more than 4.4576 mm (link5, static) or 3.9559 mm (gripper_link, over q5 in [0, 88.31] deg) past the plane z=115.428 mm within r<=30 mm of the link5 z-axis.' P1 as asserted: 'the authoring source STL contains no distal jaw finger geometry.' THE GAP, in five separable pieces. (i) THRESHOLD vs PRESENCE. L_MIN=5.5 mm is a VIABILITY floor, derived in the script header (L22-27) as x = L - m with m = 5.5 mm margin and T1-real grip depth x in (0,12] mm. FAIL therefore means 'this material cannot yield an operationally usable grip depth', not 'this material does not exist'. The script itself states the correct proposition at L26-27 — 'Source geometry shallower than this cannot yield an in-range L' — which presupposes that geometry EXISTS and is merely shallow. The prose escalates 'shallow' to 'absent'. (ii) The escalation is not academic: the fixed body's 4.4576 mm is only 0.0424 mm below the alternative D426 G-e floor of 4.5 mm that the gate_contract text explicitly names and declines to use. Against that floor the fixed body is inside the preregistered sweep error bound (0.198 mm) of the boundary. The 'ABSENT' label is a function of which of two documented floors was pinned. Q6 — Mechanisms in the script that could hide a genuinely present finger, most to least material. (1) TCP CONSTANT, GATED ONLY AGAINST ITSELF (L144, L452): the reference plane is one authored scalar; GV2 compares it to the URDF value it was copied from. A physically mis-placed `link5_to_hand_tcp` shifts every depth uniformly. Sensitivity: +0.55 mm clears the fixed body of FAIL, +1.55 mm makes it PASS. This is the single largest unverified lever, and nothing in this audit or in D427 constrains it. (2) URDF COVERAGE IS HARDCODED, NOT DISCOVERED: `parse_urdf()` (L356-368) skips every link not in VIS_PINS, and reads `link.find('visual')` — the FIRST `<visual>` child only. URDF permits multiple `<visual>` elements per link; a finger authored as a second visual on link5 or gripper_link would be neither loaded nor flagged, and GV2 would still pass on the first. Whether the URDF actually has extra visuals or extra jaw links is UNKNOWN — I did not open it (not in the allowed read set), and critically the sealed JSON cannot answer it either, because it only records the two pinned entries. (3) DEAD-ASSET EXCLUSION BY POLICY: gripper_left_link.stl is sha-recorded with `used:false`. If finger geometry lives there, the audit is blind to it by construction, not by evidence. This is exactly the 32nd-session lead. (4) WINDOW RADIUS CLIPPING (r<=30 mm): the JSON shows the clip is ACTIVE at mid-sweep — `anchors['60.0000'].r_at_l_vis_mm = 29.995` and `anchors['45.0000'].r_at_l_vis_mm = 29.982`, i.e. at those poses the argmax sits flush against the window wall, so deeper material just outside r=30 mm would be invisible. At the verdict poses (r_at = 10.12 and 0.11 mm) the clip is not binding, which limits the damage — but the metric is structurally blind beyond 30 mm at every pose. (5) SWEEP RANGE INCOMPLETE AT THE OPEN END: the grid runs [0, 88.3100] deg while the USD limits recorded in `frames.joint_limits_deg` are [0, 90.0117] — 1.70 deg of the authored range is never sampled. `coarse_l_vis_mm` is monotone decreasing toward the open end (-52.885 at 88.31), so the global max is almost certainly not there, but strictly it is unswept. (6) SINGLE ARTICULATION: only `link5_to_gripper_link` is swept. Any other DOF, and any second moving finger not modelled as this one body, is outside the experiment. (7) MAX-ONLY AGGREGATION: one scalar per pose; a finger whose material is entirely above the plane returns a negative l_vis and is indistinguishable from no material at all. (8) TASK-DIRECTION FRAMING: depth is measured only along +z. A jaw feature designed to engage laterally (side-approach) contributes nothing to l_vis no matter how large. (9) MINOR / PROPERLY HANDLED: 0.5 mm surface pitch bounds in-triangle miss to <~0.3 mm; coarse/refine angular understatement is preregistered at 0.198 / 0.0159 mm and both FAIL margins (0.542 / 1.044 mm) exceed it, so the tri-state is not boundary-adjacent under its own error model; `load_binary_stl` would abort rather than silently truncate; float32 STL precision is ~1e-3 mm at this scale. (10) REPORTING NUANCE, NOT A BLIND SPOT: for the fixed body `peak_point()` is called with the link5 point array as BOTH tool and body argument (L510), so `fixed_link5.peak_point.body_frame_m` is a duplicate of `tool_frame_m` and carries no independent information — visible in the JSON where the two arrays are byte-identical.

Cross-check on a prose claim that the JSON does not fully support: 31st doc L52-53 and D427 L25486-25487 both say the rim band (depth 5-15 mm) was empty '양 body 전 포즈' / 'all poses'. `n_pts_in_rim_band` is only computed inside `body_metrics()`, which runs at 8 poses total (link5 static, moving refined peak, and the 6 anchors) — the 354-pose coarse loop (L523-528) computes only l_vis and the wall max. Within r<=30 mm the all-pose claim IS entailed transitively (rim needs depth>=5 and l_vis<5 everywhere), but the rim mask has no radius restriction, so the ALL-RADII reading of that sentence is verified at 8 poses, not 354. Minor, but it is the kind of over-generalisation this audit is meant to catch.

reasoning: FRAME RECONSTRUCTION VERIFIED FIRST. From URDF joint `link5_to_gripper_link` (origin xyz=0, 0.018821, 0.052035; rpy=-1.5708,-1.5708,0; axis=0 0 1) and `link5_to_hand_tcp` (z=0.115428) I rebuilt the gripper->link5 transform and reproduced the sealed JSON's moving peak point to 6e-9 m residual. Joint axis in link5 frame = (4e-6, 1, 0), i.e. perpendicular to the tool axis; joint origin x = 0 EXACTLY, so the tool axis lies inside the jaw's rotation plane. Everything below follows from that verified model, not from assumption.

CLOSED-FORM DEPTH LAW. For any material point at pivot-radius rho and body azimuth delta: depth(q5) = -63.393 mm + rho*cos(q5 - delta). Therefore the maximum depth a point can EVER reach, at any closing angle, is (rho - 63.393) mm. Reaching the TCP plane at all requires rho >= 63.393 mm; reaching L_MIN = 5.5 mm requires rho >= 68.893 mm. This converts the whole gate into a single question about pivot-radius.

MEASURED EXTREME = 67.349 mm, NOT A PLATE. The verdict-driving peak point's recorded body_frame_m = (67.083, -5.983, -18.934) mm gives rho = 67.349 mm, delta = 5.097 deg, and predicts max depth 3.9559 mm at q5 = 5.097 deg — matching the sealed refined peak (3.9559 mm @ q5=5.10) to four decimals. A mesh whose material were confined to rho <= 30 mm (a mounting plate) would yield l_vis <= -33.393 mm at EVERY q5. The observed +3.956 mm exceeds that plate-only ceiling by 37.3 mm. Plate-only is excluded by a 37 mm margin, not by a judgement call.

THE ANCHORS TRACE A SINGLE BLADE-TIP ARC. For all 125 coarse-sweep samples with q5 <= 31 deg, the measured l_vis(q5) equals the single rigid point at (rho=67.349, delta=5.097) with max |residual| = 0.000108 mm. One vertex being the support-function maximizer over a >=31 deg direction fan means a pointed/rounded tip with a wide normal cone — a tip, not a face. At q5 ~= 5 deg that tip lands at r = 0.11 mm, i.e. ON the tool axis, 3.956 mm past the TCP: the closing contact point of a jaw. A bracket or linkage does not close onto the tool axis.

THE r <= 30 mm WINDOW IS CLIPPING AT THE OPEN ANCHORS, AND THAT INVERTS THEIR MEANING. r_tip(q5) crosses 30 mm at q5 = 31.55 deg; above that the tip is outside the window and the reported argmax slides proximally along the blade. This is visible in the sealed JSON as boundary saturation: r_at_l_vis = 29.982 mm at q5=45 and 29.995 mm at q5=60. Inverting those pins gives the winning point's pivot-radius: 31.8 / 34.4 / 38.2 / 44.5 / 48.5 / 53.9 / 61.1 / 66.3 mm at q5 = 88.31 / 70 / 60 / 50 / 45 / 40 / 35 / 32 deg, with azimuth converging monotonically onto the tip's 5.1 deg. That is a continuous slender radial member running from ~32 mm to 67 mm from the pivot. Read correctly, the open anchors are positive evidence FOR a long blade.

BUT THE CLIPPING DOES NOT CHANGE THE VERDICT. At the verdict pose (q5=5.10) the argmax sits at r = 0.11 mm, 29.9 mm inside the window boundary — unclipped. Independent unwindowed confirmation: `t3_jaw_audit3_parts.csv` applies no r window, and its part_060 reproduces my tip model to <= 0.0005 mm at all four sampled angles INCLUDING r = 43.21 mm (q5=45) and r = 66.88 mm (q5=88.31); its unwindowed max depth over 64 parts x 4 angles is 3.690 mm. The only material the window can permanently hide is that with body-axial z > +11.18 mm, which lies >= 30 mm laterally from the tool axis and cannot contact a D29 (r=14.5 mm) cylinder. So the narrower operational fact the claim states — no jaw material reaches >= 5.5 mm below the TCP plane within r <= 30 mm at any closing angle — is exactly and robustly what Gate-0 established. The numeric verdict FAIL is correct; the margin (1.544 mm of pivot-radius) is far above the preregistered error bounds.

THE COLLISION LAYER HAS THE BLADE TOO. parts 060/061/063 in the sealed audit3 CSV all track the same tip trajectory. So 31st §5-4's stronger sentence — '실물 그리퍼에는 있는 원위 손가락이 자산(시각+충돌)에는 없다' — is contradicted at BOTH layers by the project's own sealed artifacts.

THE '시각적으로 명백' STEP IS A VIEWPOINT ARTIFACT. `gate0/gripper_vis` is logged non-static at 6 sweep_index values, so a Rerun 3D view can display at most ONE pose at a time. I measured the sealed inspection PNG's time cursor two independent ways — cursor x-fraction 0.0761 of the plot data range -> index 26.9, and the q5 curve height at the cursor -> 81.5 deg — both giving sweep_index ~= 27. The last gripper log at or before index 27 is index 0 = q5 = 88.31 deg = FULLY OPEN (next anchor is index 113). Confirmation by pixel geometry: the lowest blue pixel in the 3D panel corresponds to 52.75 mm ABOVE the TCP versus l_vis(88.31) = 52.885 mm above — a 1-pixel match; rightmost blue = 73.1 mm lateral versus the tip's predicted 66.9 mm (x1.09 perspective magnification, object nearer camera). Zero blue pixels exist anywhere below y=758, i.e. nowhere near the L_MIN rings — necessarily so, because in the fully-open pose the jaw is swung 88 deg away by construction. That frame has zero discriminating power on finger presence/absence. And the '수평 플레이트 형상' that was described IS the blade: my native-resolution crop of the blue cloud shows a servo-horn plate (central circle with lobed satellites) plus a long tapered arm with an elongated through-slot and a rounded tip, lying horizontal because it is fully open.

INDEPENDENT CORROBORATION FROM THE PHOTOGRAMMETRY LENS. That lens measured plate height 43 mm, blade free length 41 mm, servo-horn circle near the plate centre (=> pivot-to-tip ~62-68 mm), blade outer span 38.6 mm, sheet 1.5 mm. The sealed asset gives rho_tip = 67.349 mm and an along-pivot-axis bbox extent of 39.37 mm. Both bracket/match. The rotation-plane bbox is 77.85 x 25.24 mm (aspect 3.08) — a 67 mm reach inside a 25 mm-wide band is a blade by any definition.

WHAT THE WORDING SHOULD HAVE SAID. Both jaws DO have material below the TCP plane: moving 3.956 mm, fixed 4.458 mm. Nothing is 'absent'. The honest statement is a radial shortfall: the moving jaw's distal blade tip sits at rho = 67.349 mm, which is 1.544 mm short of the 68.893 mm needed for L_MIN = 5.5 mm, and 5.544 / 9.544 mm short of the 72.893 / 76.893 mm needed for the recommended L band [9.5, 13.5] mm. That reframes the 수제 저작 branch from 'author a finger the source does not have' to 'lengthen an existing 67.3 mm blade by ~1.5 mm (gate) or ~5.5-9.5 mm (recommended band)' — and it reopens the question D427 implication ② closed off, namely why the collision cook/decomposition yields an occluded jaw when the blade is demonstrably present in both layers. So the claim's core assertion — that the wording is not literally supported and the branch premise must be re-checked before approval — holds.

VERDICT: NOT REFUTED. The claim's two substantive parts are both confirmed by re-derivation from the sealed artifacts alone: (i) the visual authoring source does contain the moving jaw's long distal blade (rho = 67.349 mm, verified to 1e-4 mm across 125 sweep samples and to 5e-4 mm across 4 collision angles), and (ii) what Gate-0 measured is the narrower depth/window fact, correctly stated. verdicts.strongest_counterevidence: The strongest case AGAINST the claim is semantic-plus-empirical, and it does not come from the photos at all. In `t3r_gate0_vismesh_bands.csv` (sealed, read-only) the moving jaw has ZERO sampled points in the rim band (depth 5–15 mm) at every pose, and `t3r_gate0_vismesh_results.json` gives max_depth_in_wall_annulus (12.5–20 mm) = 2.795 mm. At the closed poses the only moving-jaw material below the TCP plane is confined to r <= 13.40 mm (q5=0) / 12.36 mm (q5=5.1 deg) — i.e. near-axis, plug-analog, not a jaw wall. So whatever tine geometry gripper_link.stl contains, none of it presents a usable finger wall anywhere near the L_MIN plane. If this project uses "원위 손가락 / distal jaw finger" as a functional term of art meaning "jaw wall material reaching the L_MIN band", then D427 implication (1) is internally consistent and the claim reduces to a wording quibble rather than a substantive error. A second, weaker counterpoint: I never opened gripper_link.stl (banned), so my statement that the mesh contains long tines rests on two derived project artifacts — the bbox 77.85 x 25.24 x 39.37 mm recorded in the results JSON, and the blue point cloud in t3r_gate0_vismesh_inspection.png — not on the STL itself.
reasoning: EXIF is decisive and was not used by the photogrammetric lens. All six frames: Samsung SM-S906N, FocalLength 5.4 mm, FocalLengthIn35mmFilm 23 mm, f/1.8, DigitalZoomRatio 1.0, raw 4000x3000 with EXIF orientation 8. That pins f_px = 2658 px (diagonal convention) or 2700 px (2.0 um binned pitch of the ISOCELL GN5) — adopt 2660 +/- 2%.

Object distance is therefore D = f_px / scale, i.e. VERY close: p02 D=132 mm, p00 D=134 mm, p04 D=145 mm (left end) to 157 mm (right end). These are hand-held macro-range shots, at or just beyond the phone's minimum focus. The worst-case parallax gradient is 1/D = 0.64–0.76 %/mm of out-of-plane relief — roughly TWICE the 0.4 %/mm the photogrammetric lens estimated, and its 0.4 %/mm was itself derived from an assumption (that the two tines are parallel) that I show below is false.

I re-derived every scale myself. p02: 76 clean 1 mm ticks, median pitch 20.11 px, sub-pixel; segment autocorrelation gives 20.000 px/mm at y=400 rising to 20.169 at y=1450 (2.2% gradient). p00 (tilted ruler, band x 2060–2140): 19.58 px/mm at y=1550 to 20.02 at y=2150. p04: 18.024 / 17.432 / 16.827 / 16.320 / 15.766 px/mm at x = 1075 / 1625 / 2225 / 2825 / 3425 — a MONOTONE 14.3% gradient across the ruler. sqrt(1/s) is linear in x to better than 0.3%, confirming the 1-D projective model, so I could integrate the scale rather than pick one.

The '~78 mm' number is a scale-choice artifact. In p04 the part silhouette (T=90, largest component) spans x = 741..2139 = 1398 px. Over that span the ruler's own local scale runs 18.382 -> 16.944 px/mm (8.5%). The SAME 1398 px reads: 77.56 mm (scale at the left end), 79.26 mm (properly integrated — my best value), 81.87 mm (whole-ruler median 17.076), 83.08 mm (scale at the right end). The mesh bbox X = 77.85 mm sits INSIDE that interval. Reporting 78.5 mm and calling it a match to 77.85 mm is choosing the scale that lands on the answer.

Cross-photo dispersion confirms it. My own long-axis values: p04 79.26 mm, p00 82.15 mm (dy 82.15 + dx 26.88 -> hull 86.44), p02 84.42 mm (x-span 1706 px at 20.21 px/mm; hull diameter 91.29 mm). Mean 81.94, sd 2.59 mm = 3.2%, on the same part, same rule, same method. The claimed agreement is 0.15 mm = 0.19% — about 17x tighter than the method's own 1-sigma, before any bias term.

I demonstrated the coincidence directly by finding a SECOND, mutually incompatible 'match' in the same dataset: p02 convex-hull diameter 91.29 mm vs the mesh bbox diagonal 90.82 mm — a 0.5% agreement, just as impressive as 78 vs 77.85, but implying a different correspondence. When a method with 7% spread yields two contradictory sub-1% 'agreements', both are noise.

Out-of-plane relief is the dominant, unbounded bias and the photo set cannot constrain it. In p04 the two silhouette endpoints are at 385 px and 668 px above the ruler line — neither is in the ruler plane. I tried three independent ways to pin the camera elevation and got mutually inconsistent answers: (a) tick-line vanishing point — slopes sd 0.074 over a 66 px baseline, pure noise, unusable; (b) the two-tine tip differential (lower tine tip x=2120 at the ruler, upper tine tip x=2138 elevated) implies only ~1.3% magnification difference, i.e. elevation ~3 deg; (c) ruler-face foreshortening (apparent width 600 px / 16.3 px/mm = 36.8 mm in p04 vs 37.3 mm in p02) implies almost no foreshortening at all. These cannot all be true. THAT INCONSISTENCY IS THE FINDING: the six photos do not contain enough constraint to certify the parallax bias small. At D=140 mm the worst case is +7.7% for 10 mm of relief, +21.7% for 25 mm, +38.6% for 39 mm — i.e. up to +17 to +31 mm on an 80 mm span, one-signed (always inflating).

Error scaling behaves exactly as a perspective-gradient error should, which validates the diagnosis. I measured the SAME manufactured feature — the servo-horn central bore, via largest-inscribed-circle on a common threshold — in three photos: 163.1 px (p00), 170.8 px (p02), 153.9 px (p04), which with each photo's local scale give 8.35 / 8.45 / 8.53 mm, a 2.2% spread. Small features (160 px) are reproducible; long spans (1400–1700 px) disperse by 7%. Error proportional to span length = scale-gradient error, not random noise.

The part is measurably deformed or non-symmetric, which independently forbids CAD-to-photo dimensional comparison. In p05 the left tine's apparent width is ~5.9 mm and the right tine's ~2.2 mm. Their offsets from the principal point are -760 px and -85 px, i.e. viewing-ray obliquities of 16.0 deg and 1.8 deg — perspective can explain at most 14.2 deg of angular difference. Solving apparent = w*sin(a)+t*cos(a) with t=1.5 mm and w=6.5–7.6 mm needs a_left ~ 36–43 deg. That is 20–30 deg more non-parallelism than the camera geometry allows. Either the jaw is bent (very plausible for 1.5 mm sheet after disassembly) or the tines are splayed by design. Either way the as-photographed shape is not the as-authored shape.

PART IDENTITY: I challenged it and it SURVIVES — but on shape signature, not on length. I compared the photos against the repo's own sealed render t3r_gate0_vismesh_inspection.png (panel 2, blue = gripper visual per the panel-1 legend). The blue point cloud shows the identical distinctive signature: a chevron plate carrying a servo-horn bore pattern (central circle plus four lobed satellites in a cross), and two long tapered tines each with an elongated through-slot and a rounded tip. Every one of those features is present in p00/p02/p04/p05. The measured across-tine width 37.0–38.6 mm is also close to the mesh's 39.37 mm bbox dimension. Residual caveats, honestly: (i) no photo shows the part mounted on the robot; (ii) a photo cannot distinguish a left/right mirror pair, and the repo does contain a banned dead asset gripper_left_link.stl; (iii) the out-of-plane depth the photogrammetric lens could only estimate (6–8 mm, LOW confidence) does not match the mesh's 25.24 mm middle bbox dimension, and that discrepancy is UNRESOLVED — no photo shows the plate edge-on against the rule.

NET EFFECT ON THE CLAIM: the photo half of the claim is invalid and must be struck — 'physical ~78 mm vs mesh 77.85 mm' is not evidence of anything. But the claim does not depend on it. Its core assertion is checkable entirely from frozen, non-photographic evidence that I read directly: gripper_link.stl's recorded bbox is 77.85 x 25.24 x 39.37 mm (a plate-only part would be ~43 mm long), and the sealed render visibly shows two long tines. Meanwhile the gate measured exactly what the claim says it measured: l_vis = max depth BELOW the TCP plane within r <= 30 mm, peak 3.9559 mm at q5=5.10 deg for the moving jaw and 4.4576 mm for fixed link5, against L_MIN=5.5 mm. D427's Evidence block is careful ('L_MIN 벽 환형 대역에 도달하는 메시 재질 전무'), but its Implication (1) generalises that to '저작 소스(시각 STL) 자체에 원위 손가락이 없다', which is a strictly broader statement than the measurement supports.

Neither fact overturns the FAIL verdict, but both show the measurement is narrower than 'the source has no finger'.

## 2. Gate-0 증거가 실제로 세운 명제 (가장 방어 가능한 한 문장)

> **세움**: 봉인 스윕 전 구간에서, 공구축 r ≤ 30 mm 창 안에 TCP 평면보다 5.5 mm 아래로 내려가는 메시 재질은 양 body 모두 없다. 이동 조의 창 내 최심점은 **축 위(r=0.11mm)의 부리 끝 3.9559mm**, 고정측 최심점은 **r=10.12–11.50mm의 근축 구조 4.4576mm**이다. (= 33rd가 명명한 **P2**)
>
> **세우지 않음**: "소스에 원위 손가락이 없다"(**P1**). 측정된 3.9559mm는 재질 부재의 산물이 아니라 **ρ_tip 67.349 − R_TCP 63.393의 산술 결과**다. 부재였다면 이 항등식이 소수 5자리로 맞을 수 없다.

### 그리고 아무도 명시하지 않은, 결정을 실제로 지배하는 사실

깊이 지표를 **근축**이 아니라 **원통 벽면(r=14.5mm)**에서 읽으면:

```
이동 조 팁이 r=14.5 에 올 때 깊이           = +2.376 mm  (q5 ≈ 17.5°)
고정측 최심 구조 (r=10.12–11.50, 원통 footprint 안) = +4.458 mm
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
순 측벽 물림 = 2.376 − 4.458                =  −2.081 mm
```

즉 **하강하면 고정측 근축 구조가 원통 상면에 먼저 닿고, 그 시점에 이동 조 팁은 상면보다 2.08 mm 위에 있다.** 조가 측벽에 닿는 q5는 존재하지 않는다.

이 예측은 **물리 런과 독립적으로 일치**한다 — D424 attempt1/4 정지 z = top + **4.4 mm** ↔ 내가 기하로 계산한 4.458 mm. 3중 삼각측량(URDF 상수 / 봉인 bands / 물리 정지 높이).

**함의**: L_MIN 게이트를 통과시켜도(블레이드 +1.544mm) 그 argmax는 **r=0.11mm 축 위**라 원통 상면 위 허공이다. **게이트 통과 ≠ 파지 가능.** 봉인 JSON의 `manual_review_rule`("r_at_l_vis < 12.5mm는 plug-analog, 수동 검토 필요")이 이미 이 함정을 예고했고, 양 body 피크가 **둘 다** 그 조건에 걸린다.
